title: Start Here: Your Python and JavaScript Bridge
summary: Refresh what you already know, then attach the new syntax to familiar ideas. You do not need to become an expert in three languages before understanding OOP questions.

title: C Foundations: Read a Program Without Guessing
summary: C has no built-in class, inheritance or virtual keywords. Learn its typed variables, control flow, functions, arrays, pointers and structs first; these make C++ code far less intimidating.

title: C++ Syntax, References and Expressions
summary: Learn the symbols that appear repeatedly in the MCQs: std::, cout, &, *, ->, references, sizeof, comma expressions and default arguments.

title: Java Syntax and Reference Variables
summary: Read Java from the outside in: class, main, types, references, methods and access. Similar-looking C++ punctuation is not automatically valid Java.

title: Classes, Objects, Members and Nested Classes
summary: Turn the blueprint metaphor into concrete declarations. Separate a class definition, an object, a pointer/reference, and a method call.

title: Constructors: Initialization, Defaults and Copies
summary: Follow object creation one step at a time. Learn what the compiler supplies, what it does not supply, and why a constructor is not an ordinary returning function.

title: Memory, Destructors, Copying and Object Lifetime
summary: Separate the object's lifetime from the lifetime of a pointer variable. This prevents many of the most serious mistakes in the assignments.

title: Access Control: Keep the Language Label
summary: Learn exactly what public, private, protected and omitted modifiers mean. Do not transfer C++ defaults into Java or Python.

title: Encapsulation and Abstraction, Without Confusing Them
summary: Use an account with a rule: its balance must not become negative. A getter/setter pair is not automatically a safe design; the operations must preserve the rule.

title: Inheritance Shapes, Access and the Diamond
summary: Separate three questions: the shape of the hierarchy, the accessibility of inherited operations, and which implementation a call selects.

title: Overloading: Pick by the Parameters
summary: Overloading chooses among several declarations with one name. Follow the argument types before thinking about the returned value.

title: Overriding, Virtual Calls and Name Hiding
summary: For every call, write down the handle's declared type, the actual object's type, and whether the operation is virtual. Those three facts solve most polymorphism output questions.

title: Abstract Classes, Pure Virtuals and Interfaces
summary: An abstract type can define a contract without being directly constructible. An abstract base pointer is not an abstract base object.

title: this, self, super and Method Chaining
summary: Use the current object to resolve names, then distinguish a parent-qualified operation from a runtime virtual call.

title: Static Members, Local Statics and Shared State
summary: The word static has several contexts. First ask whether it describes a local variable, a file-scope name, a class field, or a member function.

title: const, final and Read-Only Views
summary: Read exactly what is protected: a value, a pointer, an object's observable state, a method override, or a class's inheritance. Similar words do different jobs.

title: Templates, Generics and Duck Typing
summary: Reuse an algorithm across types, but keep the three languages' mechanisms distinct. Generic does not mean every operation works on every possible type.

title: Inline, Friend Functions and Friend Classes
summary: Keep performance hints separate from language permissions. inline does not mean 'must be faster', and friend does not mean 'a member of this class'.

title: Exceptions: Follow the Normal Path and Error Path
summary: The supplied syllabus lists exceptions but does not develop them into a full chapter. This added foundation fills that gap and explains the assignment questions.

title: Output Questions: A Safe Step-by-Step Method
summary: Classify the program before calculating an output. A compiler error, undefined behavior, an implementation-specific assumption and a normal result are different answers.
